cards.hook: A microwave door must pass visible light while containing microwave radiation.
cards.question: How does the metal mesh in a microwave door permit a view of the food while containing microwaves?
choices: Its holes pass light but block microwaves
cards.canonicalAnswer: Its holes pass light but block microwaves
cards.revealHeadline: The openings pass visible light but block microwaves.
cards.explanation: Visible-light wavelengths pass through the small openings. Much longer microwave wavelengths are reflected by the conductive screen.

sources.title: Why Can't We Put Metal Objects in a Microwave?

cards.hook: Many fuel gauges show the location of the fuel-filler door.
cards.question: What does the arrow beside the fuel-pump icon on many dashboards indicate?
choices: Which side has the filler door
cards.canonicalAnswer: Which side has the filler door
cards.revealHeadline: The arrow points to the side with the fuel-filler door.
cards.explanation: The arrow points toward the vehicle's fuel-filler door. It provides a quick reference when driving an unfamiliar vehicle.

cards.hook: The end hook on a tape measure is deliberately movable.
cards.question: Why is the metal hook at the end of a tape measure designed to slide slightly?
cards.revealHeadline: The hook's movement compensates for its thickness.
cards.explanation: For an outside measurement, the hook moves outward; for an inside measurement, it moves inward. The travel equals the hook's thickness, keeping both readings accurate.

sources.title: Why Does the Hook on My Tape Measure Move?

cards.hook: Reeded coin edges originally made tampering visible.
cards.question: Why were ridges added to the edges of precious-metal coins?
choices: Reveal if metal was clipped away
Make a clearer ring when dropped
cards.canonicalAnswer: Reveal if metal was clipped away
cards.revealHeadline: Reeded edges revealed when metal had been removed.
cards.explanation: People once clipped valuable silver or gold from smooth coin edges. Milled or reeded patterns made missing metal visible and helped deter the practice.

sources.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
sources.title: Crisis Chronicles: The 'Not So Great' Re-Coinage of 1696

decks.title: Internet Origins
decks.description: The origins of ten familiar internet terms, symbols, and systems.

cards.hook: CAPTCHA includes a reference to a foundational test of machine intelligence.
cards.question: In the acronym CAPTCHA, the letter T honors which idea?
cards.revealHeadline: The T in CAPTCHA stands for Turing test.
cards.explanation: CAPTCHA expands to “Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart.” The acronym states the system's purpose directly.

sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.title: CAPTCHA — Glossary

cards.hook: The term spam for unwanted messages came from a comedy sketch.
cards.question: Which comedy sketch supplied the term “spam” for unwanted digital messages?
cards.revealHeadline: The term came from a Monty Python sketch centered on repeated Spam.
cards.explanation: In the Monty Python sketch, repeated servings and chants of Spam overwhelm the conversation. Online users adopted the name for unwanted messages that had a similar effect.

sources.title: RFC 2635 — DON'T SPEW: A Set of Guidelines for Mass Unsolicited Mailings and Postings
How Junk Email Came to Be Called 'Spam'

cards.hook: The first webcam monitored a shared workplace resource.
cards.question: Which object did Cambridge researchers monitor with the first webcam?
cards.revealHeadline: The first webcam monitored the Trojan Room coffee pot.
cards.explanation: Researchers watched the Trojan Room coffee pot from their desks to avoid an unnecessary trip when it was empty. The feed was later made available on the internet.

sources.title: The Trojan Room Coffee Pot Timeline

cards.hook: The @ symbol supplied a clear separator for network email.
cards.question: Ray Tomlinson placed @ inside email addresses mainly because it did what?
cards.revealHeadline: The @ sign expressed a user at a host computer.
cards.explanation: Tomlinson needed a separator that was not normally used in names. @ was available and locative: it neatly expressed a person “at” a particular computer.

cards.hook: The first public website documented the system it used.
cards.question: A visitor to the world's first website would mainly learn about which subject?
cards.revealHeadline: The first website explained the World Wide Web project.
cards.explanation: Hosted at info.cern.ch, the site described the World Wide Web project and explained how to create and navigate web pages.

sources.title: A Short History of the Web

cards.hook: The sideways smiley was proposed to clarify tone in plain text.
cards.question: Scott Fahlman proposed :-) on a 1982 message board to signal what?
choices: The text was meant as a joke
cards.canonicalAnswer: The text was meant as a joke
cards.revealHeadline: :-) marked a message as a joke.
cards.explanation: Fahlman suggested the sideways smile as a “joke marker,” with :-( for serious posts. The symbols helped distinguish tone in plain-text discussions.

cards.hook: The hashtag began as a convention proposed by a Twitter user.
cards.question: When Chris Messina proposed using # on Twitter in 2007, what problem was he solving?
cards.revealHeadline: The hashtag was intended to group posts by topic.
cards.explanation: Messina suggested using # plus a word to group related messages. Twitter initially declined to build it, but users made the convention spread.

sources.title: How the Hashtag Became a Way to Instantly Invite Everyone Into a Conversation

cards.hook: Before DNS, hosts repeatedly downloaded a central name-to-address file.
cards.question: Why did updates to HOSTS.TXT stop scaling as the network grew?
choices: Each host uploaded its own full copy
More hosts downloaded an ever-larger file
Every lookup crossed the network twice
cards.canonicalAnswer: More hosts downloaded an ever-larger file
cards.revealHeadline: More hosts had to download an increasingly large central file.
cards.explanation: The NIC maintained one HOSTS.TXT file that mapped names to addresses, and hosts downloaded updated copies. As the file and network grew, the traffic and central maintenance became impractical; DNS distributed the work.

sources.title: The Domain Name System: Emergence and Evolution

cards.hook: Private browsing limits local storage but does not make network activity private.
cards.question: After an incognito session closes, who may still have observed the sites visited?
cards.revealHeadline: Websites and network providers may still observe private-browsing activity.
cards.explanation: Private browsing limits history and site data saved on the device. Websites, an employer or school, and the internet service provider may still observe the activity.

cards.hook: The first ARPANET host-to-host message was interrupted after two characters.
cards.question: UCLA planned to send LOGIN over ARPANET before the remote computer crashed. What arrived?
cards.revealHeadline: The receiving computer recorded “LO.”
cards.explanation: The receiving computer received L and O, then crashed before G arrived. About an hour later, the team successfully transmitted the full word LOGIN.

sources.title: Pioneers and Visionaries to Celebrate Internet's 50th Anniversary at UCLA

decks.title: Game Design and History
decks.description: The origins and design of ten familiar games.

cards.hook: Mario first appeared in Donkey Kong under a different name.
cards.question: Before he was Mario, what was the main character of Nintendo's Donkey Kong called?
cards.revealHeadline: The character was called Jumpman.
cards.explanation: In Donkey Kong, the character was called Jumpman and worked as a carpenter. Nintendo later renamed him Mario and eventually made him a plumber.

sources.publisher: The Strong National Museum of Play
sources.title: Donkey Kong

cards.hook: The center pieces of a 3×3 Rubik's Cube remain fixed relative to one another.
cards.question: On a scrambled 3×3 Rubik's Cube, what does each fixed center piece reveal?
choices: Which color belongs on that face
cards.canonicalAnswer: Which color belongs on that face
cards.revealHeadline: Each center identifies the solved color of its face.
cards.explanation: The six center pieces stay fixed relative to one another. Each center identifies the solved color of its face, so the moving edges and corners must match it.

sources.title: Handbook of Cubik Math — Chapter 2: A Cubik Orientation

cards.hook: The name Tetris combines a geometric term with a sport.
cards.question: The name Tetris combines the Greek root for four with the name of which sport?
cards.revealHeadline: Tetris combines “tetra” with tennis.
cards.explanation: Each tetromino uses four squares, supplying the Greek “tetra.” Creator Alexey Pajitnov added tennis, his favorite sport, to complete the name.

sources.publisher: The Strong National Museum of Play
sources.title: Tetris

cards.hook: The Landlord's Game was designed as an economic argument.
cards.question: Lizzie Magie's Landlord's Game, an ancestor of Monopoly, was designed to demonstrate what?
cards.revealHeadline: The game was designed to criticize land monopolies.
cards.explanation: Magie used the Landlord's Game to illustrate how rent and concentrated land ownership enrich landlords at the expense of tenants. Monopoly later emphasized competition and property acquisition.

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
sources.title: Playing Monopoly (and Its Discontents) on Its 80th Anniversary
Lizzie Magie and the History of Monopoly

cards.hook: Scrabble's tile distribution and scores were based on letter frequency.
cards.question: Why do common letters such as E have low values while rare letters such as Q have high values in English Scrabble?
choices: Counts of letters in printed English
Lengths of letters in Morse code
Positions of letters in the alphabet
cards.canonicalAnswer: Counts of letters in printed English
cards.revealHeadline: Alfred Butts used counts of letters in printed English.
cards.explanation: Alfred Butts tallied letters in sources including newspapers. Frequent letters received more tiles and lower scores; rarer letters were scarcer and worth more.

cards.hook: UNO was initially sold through its inventor's workplace.
cards.question: Merle Robbins sold early UNO decks from his own workplace. Which workplace was it?
cards.revealHeadline: Merle Robbins sold early UNO decks in his barbershop.
cards.explanation: Robbins, a barber, developed UNO after disagreements over Crazy Eights rules. His family financed 5,000 decks, which he first sold through his shop.

sources.title: UNO Celebrates 50 Years of Bringing People Together

sources.publisher: The Strong National Museum of Play
sources.title: Uno

cards.hook: Nintendo began as a playing-card company in 1889.
cards.question: Nintendo's original business in 1889 centered on making which product?
cards.revealHeadline: Nintendo's first product was hanafuda playing cards.
cards.explanation: Fusajiro Yamauchi started Nintendo producing hanafuda, traditional Japanese playing cards. The company entered electronic games many decades later.

sources.title: Nintendo Switches Things Up With a New Museum That Embraces Nostalgia and Celebrates Gaming History

cards.hook: Twister treated players as components on the board.
cards.question: In Twister's breakthrough design, the players themselves function as what?
cards.revealHeadline: The players function as the game pieces.
cards.explanation: Reyn Guyer's floor-mat design made people serve as the playing pieces. The unfamiliar format initially made the game difficult for some retailers and shoppers to understand.

sources.publisher: The Strong National Museum of Play
sources.title: Twister
How the Classic American Game of Twister Went From Risqué to Record-Breaking

cards.hook: The queen in early European chess had limited movement.
cards.question: In medieval European chess, the piece that became the queen could usually move how?
cards.revealHeadline: The piece could move only one square diagonally.
cards.explanation: The earlier counselor or queen moved only one square diagonally. Around the late 15th century, new rules gave the piece its modern ability to move any distance along a rank, file, or diagonal.

cards.hook: A cuneiform tablet preserves rules related to the Royal Game of Ur.
cards.question: How did scholars recover rules for the ancient Royal Game of Ur?
choices: They were painted on the board
They were written on a cuneiform tablet
They were inferred from worn squares
They survived in a Greek poem
cards.canonicalAnswer: They were written on a cuneiform tablet
cards.revealHeadline: The rules were recovered from a cuneiform tablet.
cards.explanation: A Babylonian cuneiform tablet preserves rules for the twenty-squares game family. It allows modern scholars and players to reconstruct a game represented by much older boards.

sources.title: Cuneiform Tablet with Rules for the Royal Game of Ur
First Board Game with Surviving Rules

decks.title: Mathematical Patterns
decks.description: Ten results from probability, geometry, and number theory.

cards.hook: The sums of two fair dice are not equally likely.
cards.question: When two fair six-sided dice are rolled, which total can be produced by the most ordered outcomes?
cards.revealHeadline: Seven has six of the 36 possible ordered outcomes.
cards.explanation: The pairs 1+6 through 6+1 all total 7, giving six of the 36 equally likely outcomes. No other total has as many routes.

cards.hook: Even divisibility rules out primality for all but one integer.
cards.question: Which even number has exactly two positive divisors?
cards.revealHeadline: Two is the only even prime number.
cards.explanation: A prime has exactly two positive divisors: 1 and itself. Every larger even number is divisible by 2 as well, so it cannot be prime.

cards.hook: A shared birthday becomes more likely than not in a relatively small group.
cards.question: Ignoring leap day, about how many people make a shared birthday more likely than not?
cards.revealHeadline: A group of 23 people contains 253 possible pairs.
cards.explanation: The probability depends on comparing every possible pair, not one person with the rest of the group. With 23 people, 253 pairings place the chance of at least one match just above 50 percent.

cards.hook: A single half-twist changes the topology of a paper loop.
cards.question: A paper strip is joined into a loop after one half-twist. How many sides and edges does it have?
cards.revealHeadline: A Möbius strip has one continuous side and one continuous edge.
cards.explanation: Tracing the surface without lifting a finger returns to the starting point after covering what initially appeared to be both sides. The boundary forms one continuous edge as well.

sources.title: Painting — One Surface and One Edge (Möbius)

cards.hook: The repeating decimal 0.999… is an alternate notation for a familiar real number.
cards.question: On the real number line, where does the repeating decimal 0.999… land?
cards.revealHeadline: 0.999… is exactly equal to 1.
cards.explanation: Let x = 0.999…. Then 10x = 9.999…, so subtracting x gives 9x = 9 and x = 1. The two notations name the same real number.

sources.title: Is the Infinite Decimal .9999... the Same as 1?

cards.hook: The term googol was suggested by a nine-year-old.
cards.question: Who supplied mathematician Edward Kasner with the word “googol”?
cards.revealHeadline: Kasner's nephew Milton Sirotta proposed the word “googol.”
cards.explanation: Kasner asked his nine-year-old nephew Milton Sirotta to name 10¹⁰⁰. Milton proposed “googol,” a word that later inspired the spelling of Google.

cards.hook: Every planar map can be colored with a fixed maximum number of colors.
cards.question: A flat map needs at most how many colors so regions sharing a border never match?
cards.revealHeadline: Four colors are sufficient for every planar map.
cards.explanation: The four-color theorem guarantees four colors are enough when regions that share a boundary must differ. Merely touching at a corner does not count.

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
sources.title: Computer Printout, Semi-critical Subsets of Colorings of the 6-Ring
Every Planar Map Is Four Colorable

cards.hook: A taxi ride prompted a well-known observation about sums of cubes.
cards.question: One taxi number equals both 12³ + 1³ and 10³ + 9³. Which number is it?
cards.revealHeadline: 1729 is the Hardy–Ramanujan taxicab number.
cards.explanation: Hardy called his taxi number dull; Ramanujan immediately noted it is the smallest positive integer expressible as two positive cubes in two different ways.

sources.title: The Engines of Our Ingenuity: Ramanujan

cards.hook: Repeatedly ordering and subtracting four digits converges on a fixed value.
cards.question: What result does the subtraction 7641 − 1467 produce?
cards.revealHeadline: 7641 − 1467 equals 6174, the fixed point of Kaprekar's routine.
cards.explanation: Because 7641 − 1467 equals 6174, repeating the routine produces the same result. Every four-digit starting value with at least two distinct digits reaches 6174 within seven rounds.

cards.hook: Leading digits in many real-world datasets are not uniformly distributed.
cards.question: In many datasets spanning several scales, which leading digit appears about 30 percent of the time?
cards.revealHeadline: Benford's law predicts that 1 appears first about 30 percent of the time.
cards.explanation: For suitable naturally occurring datasets, 1 leads about 30.1 percent of values, while 9 leads only about 4.6 percent. The pattern is logarithmic, not uniform.

sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.title: Benford's Law

sources.publisher: Carnegie Mellon University Software Engineering Institute
sources.title: Benford's Law: Potential Applications for Insider Threat Detection

decks.title: Mythological Creatures
decks.description: Ten creatures and figures in their original mythological traditions.

cards.hook: Perseus targeted one of the three Gorgon sisters.
cards.question: Medusa had two Gorgon sisters, Stheno and Euryale. What made her uniquely vulnerable to Perseus?
cards.revealHeadline: Medusa was the only mortal Gorgon sister.
cards.explanation: Stheno and Euryale were immortal, but Medusa was mortal. That distinction made her the Gorgon whom Perseus could kill.

sources.title: Dangerous Beauty: Medusa in Classical Art — Exhibition Gallery

cards.hook: Cerberus guarded the boundary of the Greek underworld.
cards.question: In his best-known three-headed form, Cerberus guarded Hades mainly to prevent whom from crossing?
cards.revealHeadline: Cerberus prevented the dead from leaving Hades.
cards.explanation: Cerberus guarded the entrance to Hades and caught or devoured shades that tried to escape. Some ancient accounts gave him more than three heads, although three became the standard depiction.

cards.hook: Killing the Minotaur did not provide a route out of the labyrinth.
cards.question: After Theseus killed the Minotaur, Ariadne’s gift solved which remaining problem?
cards.revealHeadline: Ariadne's thread allowed Theseus to retrace his route.
cards.explanation: Theseus unrolled Ariadne's thread as he entered the labyrinth. After killing the Minotaur, he followed the line back to the exit.

sources.title: Marble Sarcophagus with the Myth of Theseus and Ariadne

cards.hook: A Norse story has Thor enter Thrym's wedding feast disguised as Freyja.
cards.question: Thor disguised himself as Freyja and entered the giant Thrym’s wedding feast to recover what?
cards.revealHeadline: Thor used the disguise to recover his stolen hammer.
cards.explanation: Thrym hid Mjölnir and demanded Freyja as his bride. Thor took her place in disguise; when the hammer was produced to bless the wedding, he seized it back.

sources.title: The Meanings of Mjölnir: Thor’s Hammer & More

cards.hook: Ancient Greek depictions of Sirens differ from later mermaid-like images.
cards.question: In ancient Greek art, Sirens were typically women combined with which animal—not fish?
cards.revealHeadline: Ancient Greek artists depicted Sirens with bird bodies.
cards.explanation: Homer never described the Sirens’ bodies, but ancient Greek artists gave them human heads and bird bodies. Their mermaid-like image developed much later.

sources.title: Dangerous Beauty: Medusa in Classical Art — Sirens
Sirens of Greek Myth Were Bird-Women, Not Mermaids

cards.hook: Chinese and European traditions assign different roles to dragons.
cards.question: In traditional Chinese imagery, a dragon was often welcomed because it could bring what?
cards.revealHeadline: Chinese dragons were associated with rain and successful harvests.
cards.explanation: Chinese dragons were often powerful but benevolent beings associated with rain and bountiful harvests. Their command of water also helped link them to imperial rule.

cards.hook: The banshee's traditional role differs from later depictions of a lethal spirit.
cards.question: In Irish folklore, hearing a banshee’s wail most often meant she was doing what?
choices: Warning that a death was near
cards.canonicalAnswer: Warning that a death was near
cards.revealHeadline: The banshee's wail warned that a death was near.
cards.explanation: Traditional accounts treat the banshee as a death omen whose wail heralds a loss, often for a particular family. She predicts the death rather than causing it.

sources.publisher: National Folklore Collection, University College Dublin

cards.hook: Ammit waited beside the scales in Egyptian representations of afterlife judgment.
cards.question: According to the Egyptian judgment scene, what happened to a heart that failed to balance against Ma'at's feather?
cards.revealHeadline: Ammit would devour a heart that failed the test.
cards.explanation: Ammit combined crocodile, lion, and hippopotamus traits. An unworthy heart was fed to her, condemning its owner to nonexistence rather than an afterlife.

sources.title: Ancient Egyptian Gods and Goddesses — Ammit

cards.hook: Medieval bestiaries paired the basilisk with an unexpected animal adversary.
cards.question: According to medieval bestiaries, which ordinary animal could hunt and kill a basilisk?
cards.revealHeadline: Medieval bestiaries identified the weasel as the basilisk's adversary.
cards.explanation: Bestiaries claimed a weasel could pursue the lethal basilisk into its hole and kill it. Writers turned the matchup into a lesson that every evil has a remedy.

sources.title: Weird and Wonderful Creatures of the Bestiary

cards.hook: Garuda is often depicted in conflict with another class of mythological beings.
cards.question: The eaglelike Garuda, mount of Vishnu, is traditionally shown fighting which beings?
cards.revealHeadline: Garuda's traditional adversaries are the serpent beings called nagas.
cards.explanation: Hindu tradition makes Garuda Vishnu’s divine vehicle and a frequent foe of nagas. One account calls them stepbrothers whose rivalry began with their mothers.

sources.publisher: Herbert F. Johnson Museum of Art, Cornell University

decks.description: Ten facts explained by scientific definitions, structures, and physical processes.

cards.hook: Scientific deserts are classified by precipitation rather than temperature.
cards.question: By total area, which place is Earth's largest desert?
cards.revealHeadline: Antarctica is Earth's largest desert.
cards.explanation: A desert is defined by scarce precipitation, not heat or sand. Antarctica receives very little snowfall and spans about 14.2 million square kilometers.

cards.hook: Botanical definitions of fruit differ from everyday usage.
cards.question: Botanically, which fruit is a true berry even though a strawberry is not?
cards.revealHeadline: A banana is botanically a berry, while a strawberry is not.
cards.explanation: A botanical berry develops from one flower with one ovary and has fleshy layers around its seeds. Bananas qualify; strawberries are aggregate accessory fruits.

sources.publisher: McGill University Office for Science and Society
sources.title: Bananas Are Berries. Raspberries Are Not.

sources.publisher: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

cards.hook: The structure of a wombat's intestine affects the shape of its droppings.
cards.question: A wombat is the only known animal to routinely leave droppings in what shape?
cards.revealHeadline: Wombats routinely produce cube-shaped droppings.
cards.explanation: Dry material and unevenly stiff regions of the intestine form the corners before exit. The flat sides may help territorial markers stay put on rocks and logs.

sources.title: Intestines of Non-Uniform Stiffness Mold the Corners of Wombat Feces

sources.publisher: Cleland Wildlife Park, Government of South Australia

cards.hook: A rainbow's apparent shape depends on the observer's position and visible droplets.
cards.question: From a vantage point high above water droplets, what complete shape can a rainbow form?
cards.revealHeadline: A rainbow can appear as a complete circle.
cards.explanation: Sunlight refracts and reflects inside water droplets. From the ground, the horizon blocks the lower part; high above droplets, a viewer may see the rainbow close into a complete circle.

cards.hook: The isotopic composition of uranium ore at Oklo required a geological explanation.
cards.question: At Oklo, ore was depleted in uranium-235 and contained fission products. What process had occurred?
choices: A meteorite had mixed into the ore
A natural fission chain reaction had run
cards.canonicalAnswer: A natural fission chain reaction had run
cards.revealHeadline: A natural fission chain reaction occurred at Oklo.
cards.explanation: About two billion years ago, uranium-rich rock at Oklo reached criticality. Groundwater slowed neutrons enough to maintain fission, leaving depleted uranium-235 and fission products behind.

sources.title: Meet Oklo, the Earth's Two-Billion-Year-Old Only Known Natural Nuclear Reactor

cards.hook: The fossil record places shark ancestors well before the first trees.
cards.question: Shark ancestors date to about 450 million years ago and the first trees to about 385 million. What is the approximate difference?
cards.revealHeadline: Shark ancestors predated the first trees by about 65 million years.
cards.explanation: Shark-like scales appear around 450 million years ago, while the first trees arrived around 385 million years ago. Subtracting the dates gives a 65-million-year gap.

sources.title: Shark Evolution: A 450 Million Year Timeline

cards.hook: Thermal expansion produces measurable changes in the Eiffel Tower.
cards.question: What movement occurs after the sun heats one side of the Eiffel Tower?
cards.revealHeadline: Solar heating makes the Eiffel Tower expand and lean away from the heat.
cards.explanation: Heat expands the iron, making the tower a few millimeters taller. Uneven heating also makes its top trace a curve about 15 centimeters across during a clear day.

sources.publisher: Société d’Exploitation de la Tour Eiffel

cards.hook: The term for the earthy scent after rain was coined from two Greek roots.
cards.question: Which word names the earthy scent after rain?
cards.revealHeadline: The word is petrichor.
cards.explanation: CSIRO chemists coined petrichor in 1964 from Greek petra, stone, and ichor, the gods’ ethereal blood. Moisture releases the characteristic scent from soil and rock.

sources.publisher: Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation
sources.title: The Smell of Rain: How Our Scientists Invented a New Word
Scent of Rain, Strands of Honey

cards.hook: Wood frogs can survive extensive freezing during winter.
cards.question: While a wood frog is frozen, what happens to its heartbeat?
choices: It speeds up and stays fast
It stops, then restarts on thawing
cards.canonicalAnswer: It stops, then restarts on thawing
cards.revealHeadline: A wood frog's heart stops during freezing and restarts during thawing.
cards.explanation: Glucose helps protect the frog's cells while much of its body freezes. Breathing and heartbeat stop; during thawing, the heart is among the first organs to resume function.

cards.hook: The triple point is a precise thermodynamic equilibrium.
cards.question: At water’s triple point, which three phases coexist in equilibrium?
cards.revealHeadline: Ice, liquid water, and water vapor coexist at the triple point.
cards.explanation: At about 0.01°C and 4.6 torr, solid, liquid, and gas coexist in equilibrium. Triple-point cells turn that precise condition into a temperature reference.

sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.title: Triple-Point Cell
